prompt: Sort each study by the approach it takes.

cards.text: Twelve lapsed gym members are asked, in open conversation, why they stopped attending.
cards.explanation: A small sample and an unstructured conversation about the reasons for behavior: qualitative research.

cards.text: A structured questionnaire estimates the share of 1,500 adults who order meal kits each month.
cards.explanation: A large sample chosen to represent a population, and a measure of how often a behavior occurs: quantitative research.

cards.text: Eight parents photograph their breakfast table every morning for a week and describe each photograph.
cards.explanation: The data consist of images and words from a small sample: qualitative research.

cards.text: A bank asks 900 customers to rate their satisfaction on a scale from 1 to 10 and compares the regions statistically.
cards.explanation: Numbers that are analyzed statistically, from a large structured sample: quantitative research.

cards.text: After a survey shows that loyalty fell among young customers, the firm holds conversations with ten of them to understand why.
cards.explanation: Qualitative research is also used after quantitative research, to interpret its findings.

cards.text: A retailer measures, across 40 stores, how far the average basket value rises during a promotion.
cards.explanation: Measuring to what extent a behavior occurs, across a large set of cases: quantitative research.

prompt: A participant in a depth interview discusses a reusable water bottle. Put the answers in the order that laddering moves through them, from the product attribute to the personal value.

steps.text: “The bottle keeps water cold all day.”
steps.explanation: Laddering begins with a product attribute: a property of the bottle itself.

steps.text: “So I no longer buy drinks while I am out.”
steps.explanation: The first consequence: what the attribute allows the participant to do.
A further consequence of the first one, one step closer to what the participant cares about.
The ladder ends at the personal value that the attribute ultimately serves.

prompt: Each case describes a task given to a participant. Name the projective technique it uses.

cases.text: The moderator says “energy drink”, and the participant says the first word that comes to mind.
cases.explanation: Responding to a word with the first word or idea that occurs: an association technique.

cases.text: The participant finishes the sentence “A man who drives an electric car is …”
cases.explanation: Completing an incomplete sentence is a completion technique.

cases.text: The participant sees a drawing of two friends at a supermarket shelf and writes what one of them is saying.
cases.explanation: Constructing the words spoken by a person in a drawing is a construction technique.

cases.text: The participant describes how a typical neighbour feels when buying the cheapest brand of coffee.
cases.explanation: Describing the feelings of another person is the third-person technique, an expressive technique.

cases.text: The participant is given the opening of a story about a family choosing a holiday and writes how it ends.
cases.explanation: Completing an incomplete story is a completion technique.

cases.text: The participant acts out the role of a salesperson trying to sell an insurance policy to a sceptical customer.
cases.explanation: Acting out a role is an expressive technique.

prompt: Each case describes a research problem. Name the qualitative method that is most appropriate.

cases.text: A snack brand has five early concepts for a new flavour and wants reactions that build on one another.
cases.explanation: Interaction among participants is expected to generate ideas in the early evaluation of concepts: a focus group.

cases.text: A bank wants to understand how customers decided to consolidate their personal debts.
cases.explanation: A sensitive topic and a complex decision: depth interviews.

cases.text: A luxury watch brand suspects that buyers are reluctant to admit that social status motivates their purchase.
cases.explanation: Participants are unlikely to state their true motives directly, so an indirect, projective technique is appropriate.

cases.text: A retailer needs to know how long shoppers spend at the coffee shelf and which packages they pick up.
cases.explanation: The behavior itself is the object of study, and shoppers cannot accurately report it: observation.

cases.text: A kitchen appliance firm wants to understand how families prepare weekday dinners in their own homes.
cases.explanation: The research requires an understanding of behavior in its everyday context: ethnography.

cases.text: A game publisher wants to understand how players discuss a new game's pricing in forums and review platforms.
cases.explanation: The relevant consumers discuss the topic in online communities: netnography.

prompt: Sort each coding decision by the approach it follows.

cards.text: Before reading the transcripts, the analyst lists codes for the five dimensions of a published model of service quality.
cards.explanation: The codes are defined in advance on the basis of theory: deductive coding.

cards.text: While reading, the analyst notices that several participants mention the smell of the store and creates a new code for it.
cards.explanation: The code is developed from the data during analysis: inductive coding.

cards.text: The team reuses the codebook from last year's study of the same product category.
cards.explanation: The codes are defined in advance, on the basis of previous research: deductive coding.

cards.text: The analyst begins with no list of codes and labels each segment with the idea it expresses.
cards.explanation: All codes are developed from the data: inductive coding.

cards.text: A coder assigns each segment one of the codes listed in the codebook, following its definitions and examples.
cards.explanation: Applying predefined codes from a codebook is deductive coding.

cards.text: Midway through the analysis, the analyst divides one broad code into two new codes that the transcripts suggest.
cards.explanation: The new codes are developed from the data during analysis: inductive coding.

question_text: A researcher records the new codes that each interview produces. Interviews 1 to 8 produced 9, 6, 4, 3, 2, 1, 1 and 0 new codes, and interviews 9 to 11 produced none. The research question is narrow and the participants are similar. What should the researcher do?
hint: Think about the definition of saturation.

options.option_text: Calculate the sample size required for a margin of error of 5%, and continue until it is reached.
options.option_explanation: Qualitative samples are not determined by statistical calculation.

options.option_text: Continue until thirty interviews have been conducted, since qualitative studies require a fixed number.
options.option_explanation: The number required depends on the diversity of the participants and the breadth of the question, not on a fixed rule.

options.option_text: Conclude that saturation has been reached, stop data collection, and report the number of new codes per interview.
options.option_explanation: Correct. Additional interviews no longer produce new codes, and the record of new codes per interview shows how saturation was assessed.

options.option_text: Stop after the first interview that produced no new codes, since one such interview proves saturation.
options.option_explanation: Interview 8 produced no new codes, but interviews 9 to 11 were needed to show that additional interviews no longer produce new codes.

prompt: A research team plans to code 300 interview transcripts with a large language model. Put the validation steps in order.

steps.text: Develop a codebook with clear definitions and examples.
steps.explanation: Everything that follows, human and AI coding alike, uses the codebook, so it comes first.

steps.text: Have two human coders code a sample of 30 transcripts independently.
steps.explanation: The human coders establish the benchmark, working independently with the codebook.

steps.text: Have the AI tool code the same 30 transcripts with the same codebook.
steps.explanation: The AI codes exactly the same sample, so that its coding can be compared with the human coding.

steps.text: Measure the agreement between the AI and the human coders, and compare it with the agreement between the two humans.
steps.explanation: The agreement among the human coders is the standard that the AI's agreement is compared with.

steps.text: Examine the segments on which they disagree, and revise the codebook or the instructions to the AI tool.
steps.explanation: The disagreements show where the definitions or the instructions need revision.

steps.text: Code all 300 transcripts with the AI tool, and report the level of agreement.
steps.explanation: The full dataset is coded only once agreement is comparable to that among the human coders, and the level is reported.

prompt: Each excerpt comes from the reasoning trace of an AI shopping agent. Code it with the category from the codebook.

cases.text: The user wants to spend as little as possible, so I will pick whichever bag of rice costs less at the checkout.
cases.explanation: The agent states that it will minimize the amount paid, regardless of quantity.

cases.text: The bags differ in size, so I need the price per kilogram before I can compare them.
cases.explanation: The agent adopts price per unit of quantity as its criterion.

cases.text: The first hotel carries a Promoted label, which suggests the platform was paid to show it, so I will not rely on its position.
cases.explanation: The agent expresses doubt about a listing because its placement may have been paid for.

cases.text: Detergent A is $11.99 and Detergent B is $12.49, so A is the better deal.
cases.explanation: The agent compares the prices alone, without the quantity in each package.

cases.text: To find the best value I will divide each price by the number of washing loads in the bottle.
cases.explanation: Price per load is a price per unit of quantity.

cases.text: This listing is marked as sponsored; its high position may reflect payment rather than quality.
cases.explanation: The agent questions the listing because the sponsorship label indicates a paid placement.
